turns.text: Okay, let's get started. Rowan, thanks for coming in. Mom, thanks for doing the log this week, I can see a lot of entries in here. I want to go through the week first and then we'll pick something to practice. Sound okay?

Yeah. I mean it was a bad week. Honestly I don't know if any of this is working. Mondays are the worst. He's on the floor every Monday and I have to get to work, and his dad is gone by seven so it's all on me.
That sounds really hard, doing mornings on your own. Let's look at Monday specifically. Rowan, can you tell me what Monday morning was like for you?
I didn't want to go. My stomach hurt.
Your stomach hurt. What were you worried would happen at school?
That I'd throw up. In class. And everybody would see it and they'd call me puke boy.
That's a really scary thought to have. Do you remember the thermometer we made, zero to ten? If you think about Monday morning on the floor by the door, how big was the worry?
Eight. Maybe eight.
Eight. That's a big one. Thank you for telling me. And Mom, I see in the log you had an eight for that morning too, so you two are seeing it the same way, which is useful.
I mean what am I supposed to do at that point, drag him? I let him stay home. I know you're going to say that's wrong.

I'm not going to say it's wrong. I'm going to say it makes sense. When he's at an eight and you have to be somewhere, staying home ends the worst of it fast, for both of you. The trouble is it also teaches the worry that school is the thing to get away from. So we want to find a smaller step that you can actually do on a weekday morning.
Fine. But it's not just mornings. The nurse calls me like every other day.
Tell me about the nurse calls.

He goes to the nurse with a stomachache, no fever, and asks to call me. Last week I left work to get him. This week I said no and he stayed, but apparently he cried and the teacher just sent him back to his desk. They could handle it better, frankly.
So one day he went home and one day he stayed. Rowan, what happened the day you stayed?
I cried a little. Then we had reading and I forgot about it kind of.
You forgot about it. That's important. The stomachache and the worry went down even though you didn't go home. Did you throw up?
No.
No. Okay. I want to also ask about Fridays, because I see spelling tests in here twice. Rowan, what's spelling like?
Mrs. Okafor gets mad when you spell stuff wrong. Not like yelling. She does a face.
She does a face. And how big is the spelling worry on the thermometer?
Like a six.
A six. So smaller than Monday mornings but still there. Mom, on the first Friday you wrote that he was off all morning, quiet, didn't eat much. Did he say what it was about?
No, he just wasn't himself. I assumed it was the test. Could have been anything with him honestly. The second Friday he asked me in the car if she'd be mad, and I said no.

Okay. So for the first Friday we don't really know what was going on, and that's fine, we'll just keep watching. The question in the car, will she be mad, that's a lot like the questions on Monday mornings, what if I throw up, will you be home. Rowan, when you ask Mom those questions, does it help?
For a little bit. Then I want to ask again.
That's exactly how worry questions work. The answer helps for a minute and then the worry wants another answer. Mom, how many times would you guess he asks on a bad morning?
Fifteen? Twenty? I lose count. I answer every single one because if I don't he gets louder.

That makes sense. Here's what I'd like to try this week, and I want to agree on it together, not just hand it to you. When Rowan asks a what-if question about throwing up or about you being home, you answer it once. The second time, you say something like, you already know what I'm going to say, and you're brave enough to handle it. And then you stop answering. Rowan, would that be okay to try?
What if I really need to ask?
You can still ask once. Mom will still answer once. The second time she's going to trust that you know the answer. Can we try that?
Okay. I guess.
And the nurse?

For the nurse, I'd suggest a plan with the school: if there's no fever and no actual vomiting, he rests ten minutes and goes back to class, and they don't call you. Would you be willing to email the nurse about that?
Yes. Gladly. I'll do it tonight.

Great. And one small step for mornings. Rowan, I'm not asking you to love Mondays. I'm asking if, this week, on the days you do go, you could walk from the car to the door by yourself, without Mom or the aide coming to get you. Just the walk.
Can Mom watch from the car?
Mom can watch from the car. Is that okay with you, Mom?
Yes, that's fine.

Okay. So three things. Mom answers a what-if question once and then says the trust line. Mom emails the nurse about the rest-and-return plan. And Rowan walks from the car to the door by himself on school days, with Mom watching from the car. Keep logging, and if you can, put a number on the nurse days too, I didn't have one for those. Good work today, Rowan.
